term: Quantization Formats (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, bitsandbytes, FP8
definition: The practical ecosystem: GPTQ and AWQ for GPU-served 4-bit models, GGUF as the llama.cpp format for CPU/edge with many quantization levels, bitsandbytes for on-the-fly 8/4-bit loading, FP8 for modern-accelerator serving.
details: The practical ecosystem: GPTQ and AWQ for GPU-served 4-bit models, GGUF as the llama.cpp format for CPU/edge with many quantization levels, bitsandbytes for on-the-fly 8/4-bit loading, FP8 for modern-accelerator serving. Choice depends on hardware and stack.

explainer.lead: These are the practical formats for serving quantized models: GPTQ and AWQ for GPU 4-bit, GGUF for CPU and edge, bitsandbytes for on-the-fly loading, and FP8 for modern accelerators. They matter because format choice constrains where and how a model can run.

tiers.eli5: Different containers for the same compressed model — some fit a laptop, some fit a big server, and you pick based on the machine you have.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers pick the format to match hardware and stack: GGUF under llama.cpp on CPU or edge, GPTQ or AWQ for GPU serving, bitsandbytes for quick 8- or 4-bit loading, FP8 on newer accelerators. The pitfall is treating formats as interchangeable — a mismatch with your hardware or runtime blocks deployment.
tiers.paperLevel: Each format defines how weights are mapped to discrete levels and stored; the practical limits are set by hardware support and by the number of quantization levels offered, with GGUF exposing many levels.

explainer.example: Running a large model on a laptop uses a GGUF file under llama.cpp, while the same model on a GPU server might be served in GPTQ or AWQ 4-bit.
